design_detail: PROSPERO-registered systematic review and meta-analysis restricted to studies that reported a period of abstinence: 31 cross-sectional studies (1008 abstinent users with methamphetamine abuse or dependence, 984 healthy controls). Tests grouped into Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) broad abilities; random-effects pooling of Hedges' g with prediction intervals; adapted QUADAS-2 risk-of-bias assessment; meta-regression and sensitivity analyses.
can_establish: How large the average differences are between abstinent users and controls by cognitive ability, how much they vary between studies (prediction intervals), and how sensitive they are to study quality and publication bias.
cannot_establish: Whether methamphetamine caused the differences (cross-sectional only; the authors say so, pp. 748–749), or the course of recovery within people.

sample.inclusion_exclusion: Methamphetamine as primary drug with a history of abuse or dependence; a reported abstinence period; healthy comparison group without stimulant abuse or dependence; valid and reliable cognitive tests; English. Excluded animal studies, case reports and commentaries (p. 742).
sample.demographics: Users: weighted age 33.4, education 12.3 years. Controls: age 34.8, education 13.9 years (p. 744; Table 1). Mean abstinence 128.8 days (SD 99.5) across 31 studies (Table 1, p. 744).
sample.selection_effects: 48% of studies did not match groups on education (p. 744). No study was rated at low risk of bias: removing 'unclear' studies would have removed all studies (p. 743). Participants retained in treatment-based samples may be healthier than dropouts (p. 749).

exposure.measurement: As in the primary studies; 15 studies did not report whether controls had urinalysis (p. 747).
exposure.polysubstance: Quantity of use, route, other drug use, personality and undiagnosed psychiatric conditions not reported in enough studies to analyse (p. 749).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Required to be reported; mean 128.8 days across studies (Table 1, p. 744).

comparison.controls: Healthy comparison participants in each study.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No premorbid ability measures; education used as a partial proxy, while noting it may underestimate premorbid ability in people who began use at school age (p. 748).

outcomes.instruments: Tests assigned to CHC broad abilities from published factor analyses by two independent raters (pp. 742–743): fluid reasoning, short-term working memory, learning efficiency, visual-spatial processing, comprehension knowledge, retrieval fluency, processing speed, reaction and decision speed, psychomotor speed.
outcomes.operationalization: Hedges' g, negative = users worse; tests within a study averaged per ability (p. 743).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Holm-Bonferroni within (and, as a secondary check, across) abilities for meta-regressions (pp. 743–744).

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 2 (p. 745), Hedges' g [95% CI; prediction interval]: fluid reasoning −0.02 [−0.46, 0.42; −2.04 to 1.45], 14 studies; short-term working memory −0.19 [−0.44, 0.06; −1.01 to 1.01], 12; learning efficiency −0.47 [−0.58, −0.37; −0.60 to −0.34], 17, I²=1%; visual-spatial processing −0.42 [−0.74, −0.11; −1.39 to 0.54], 5; comprehension knowledge −0.43 [−0.69, −0.18; −1.32 to 0.44], 12; retrieval fluency −0.32 [−0.59, −0.04; −1.18 to 0.54], 9; processing speed −0.28 [−0.52, −0.04; −1.34 to 0.78], 22; reaction and decision speed 0.00, 3 studies; psychomotor speed −0.35 [−0.65, −0.05; −1.30 to 0.60], 9. Publication bias: Egger significant for working memory (p=.05) and learning efficiency (p=.01); trim-and-fill: working memory −0.04 [−0.26, 0.18], learning efficiency −0.40 [−0.52, −0.28] (p. 745). Risk-of-bias subgroups: comprehension knowledge −0.67 in high-risk vs −0.09 in unclear-risk studies (Qbet=7.69, p=.006) (p. 745). Longer duration of use predicted larger fluid-reasoning differences (β=−0.16 per year, Holm p=.002), although fluid reasoning showed no average difference (pp. 744, 746).
analysis.covariates: Single meta-regressions for abilities with more than 10 data points.
analysis.selective_reporting: Sensitivity results in the text and in Table 6 disagree (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Limited for visual-spatial processing (5 studies) and reaction/decision speed (3).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Abstinent users score on average below controls on learning efficiency (robust: g −0.47, narrow prediction interval, little change after trim-and-fill) and, less consistently, on several other abilities whose prediction intervals all include zero; fluid reasoning, working memory and reaction speed show no reliable difference.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion that strong statements about impaired cognition in abstinent users are premature (abstract; p. 749) matches the data. The discussion groups comprehension knowledge with abilities dependent on frontostriatal circuits (p. 746); comprehension knowledge (vocabulary-type crystallized knowledge) is the kind of measure used to estimate premorbid ability (for example, reading tests used to estimate IQ, Dean et al., 2013, p. 261), and here its group difference was confined to high-risk-of-bias studies (p. 745), which fits pre-existing or educational differences better than a drug effect.

timeline.event: Earlier meta-analysis without an abstinence requirement: medium average differences
Meta-analysis of 44 studies: moderate average differences, strong publication bias
Meta-analysis of 68 later studies: larger average differences with wide prediction intervals

replication.where_it_stands: Learning and verbal memory differences are the most consistent finding across all four meta-analyses; other domains vary between reviews.

what_would_settle_it: Longitudinal cohorts with pre-use cognitive testing, or twin designs, with abstinence verified and controls matched on education and premorbid ability (pp. 748–749).

domains.note: Medline, PsycINFO and Embase to December 2017; English only; reference lists deliberately not searched (p. 742).
Two blinded screeners, κ=0.83; third rater for disagreements (p. 742).

domains.domain: List of excluded studies with reasons (critical)
domains.note: Only the included list is referenced to the supplement; supplement not read.

domains.domain: Risk of bias of individual studies (critical)
domains.note: QUADAS-2, a diagnostic-accuracy tool, adapted to selection, information and confounding bias; κ=0.87 (p. 743).
Random effects, within-study aggregation, prediction intervals.

domains.domain: Risk of bias considered in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Subgroup and sensitivity analyses by risk of bias.

domains.domain: Conflicts of interest and funding reported

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The strongest methods of the four meta-analyses (registration, prediction intervals, risk-of-bias sensitivity, publication-bias adjustment), lowered by single-person extraction, an ill-fitting risk-of-bias tool, unverified exclusion list, no funding statement, and internal inconsistencies in the sensitivity results.

key_findings.finding: 31 studies, 1008 abstinent users and 984 controls; users had 1.6 fewer years of education on average (12.3 vs 13.9).
key_findings.locator: Results, Study Selection and Characteristics; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Learning efficiency: g −0.47 (95% CI −0.58 to −0.37), prediction interval −0.60 to −0.34, I²=1%; −0.40 after trim-and-fill.
No reliable difference in fluid reasoning (g −0.02), short-term working memory (−0.19; −0.04 after trim-and-fill) or reaction and decision speed (0.00, 3 studies).
Prediction intervals include zero for every ability except learning efficiency.
No study was rated at low risk of bias; comprehension knowledge differed only in high-risk studies (−0.67 vs −0.09).
key_findings.locator: Risk of Bias (Method); Subgroup Analyses; Table 5 (p. 747)

key_findings.finding: Education discrepancy did not significantly predict effect sizes; longer duration of use predicted larger fluid-reasoning differences (β=−0.16 per unit of duration, Holm-adjusted p=.002; the Discussion reads the unit as a year, p. 747, although Table 1 reports duration of use in months).
The authors conclude that strong statements about impaired cognition in abstinent users are premature because cross-sectional designs cannot separate pre-existing differences from drug effects.

Length of abstinence significantly moderated the comprehension-knowledge difference (11 studies; Q model 27.58, p<.001; residual Q 7.70, p=.57), the only ability where it did, and survived Holm–Bonferroni correction within and across abilities; the coefficient is printed as −0.00 with its interval bounds in the wrong order, so its direction cannot be read.
key_findings.locator: Metaregression Analyses, comprehension knowledge paragraph; footnote 2; Table 4 (p. 746)

key_findings.finding: In the primary analysis six of nine abilities had 95% CIs excluding zero (learning efficiency −0.47, visual-spatial −0.42, comprehension knowledge −0.43, retrieval fluency −0.32, processing speed −0.28, psychomotor speed −0.35); only learning efficiency also had a prediction interval excluding zero and stayed significant in both sensitivity analyses and after trim-and-fill.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says removing the four abuse-or-dependence studies did not change the results but that confidence intervals for six abilities, including learning efficiency, then overlapped zero; Table 6 shows learning efficiency still clearly negative (−0.45, −0.57 to −0.34).
reporting_issues.consequence: Text and table contradict each other; the table is more plausible.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 6 the processing-speed estimate after removing those studies is printed as 0.126 with an interval of −0.467 to 0.027, which cannot contain its own point estimate.
The text reports a 95% CI of −0.04 to 0.41 for reaction and decision speed, while Table 2 prints the estimate as 0.00 with no usable interval.
reporting_issues.consequence: That ability's estimate is unreliable (3 studies, 47 users).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 counts more participants (for example 1203 users for age) than the 1008 stated in the text; the comprehension-knowledge abstinence coefficient is printed with interval bounds in the wrong order (0.0002, −0.0008).

The text says removing high-risk-of-bias studies did not change the results, while noting that the intervals for comprehension knowledge, fluid reasoning and visual-spatial processing then included zero; Table 6 also shows short-term working memory becoming significant (−0.28, −0.52 to −0.04), which the text does not mention.
reporting_issues.consequence: This sensitivity analysis changes the conclusion for three abilities (two lose and one gains significance); describing the findings as robust overstates it.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1's standard deviations (education 0.91 and 1.43 years; duration of use 5.3 months) are implausibly small for participant-level data and appear to be standard deviations of study means; the education difference reported as d=1.31 is reproduced from them.
reporting_issues.consequence: d=1.31 should not be read as the size of the individual-level education gap; the 1.6-year mean difference is the usable figure.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 739–753 (all pages; Tables 1–2 read on the rendered pages; supplementary files not read)

disagreements.first_pass: Education discrepancy did not significantly predict effect sizes; longer duration of use predicted larger fluid-reasoning differences (β=−0.16 per year).
disagreements.reviewer: Confirmed; units are uncertain: Table 1 gives duration of use in months, while the Discussion reads β=−0.16 as per year (p. 747).
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed: Table 1 (p. 744) gives length of use in months; the Discussion (p. 747) reads the coefficient per year. Finding reworded so it does not assert the unit.

disagreements.reviewer: Missed: length of abstinence significantly moderated the comprehension-knowledge difference (Q model 27.58, p<.001; survives Holm–Bonferroni), the only ability where it did (pp. 744, 746).
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on p. 744 (text and footnote 2) and in Table 4 (p. 746). Added as a key finding because the claim on abstinence states that abstinence did not moderate group differences.

disagreements.reviewer: Missed: the primary analysis found six abilities with intervals excluding zero (Table 2, p. 745); the card should state the criterion behind 'reliable difference only for learning efficiency' so the claim can cite it.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed against Table 2 (p. 745) and Table 6 (p. 747). Added as a key finding that states both results and the criterion.

disagreements.reviewer: Confirmed reporting issue 0, with a note: the text on high-risk-of-bias removal also says the results did not change (p. 745), while Table 6 shows visual-spatial and comprehension knowledge losing significance and short-term working memory gaining it. Missed: short-term working memory became significant once high-risk studies were removed.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed against Table 6 (p. 747). Added as a separate reporting issue (the existing one concerns the abuse-or-dependence sensitivity analysis).

disagreements.reviewer: Missed: the education effect size d=1.31 (p. 744) appears to use the standard deviations of study means (0.91 and 1.43 years), not participant-level SDs.
disagreements.resolution: Recomputed: (13.88−12.31)/1.20 = 1.31 from the Table 1 SDs. Added, worded as an inference (the table does not say what its SDs describe).
